By Cody Atkinson

By Sean Lawson

Topic:AFL

The AFL has called on teams to perform to their merit ahead of finals. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

For some, to lose sometimes is better than winning — especially if the loss is a late season dead rubber and the win is a premiership.

Tension between the present and the future exists throughout society. Buy now, pay later deals are peddled readily. Conversely, saving for the future has been a staple of financial advice for generations, even if it means being more parsimonious in the short term.

Football is no different. Not all wins are the same. For some, winning now can even be an obstacle for winning later.

These thoughts came to a head last Thursday night on AFL Nation when host Gerard Whateley asked AFL executive general manager football performance Greg Swann a pointed question; whether the AFL had a policy to prevent a team mass resting players if they were locked into position for finals.

Swann's response — after a pregnant pause — was short.

"Yeah … I think we do. I'd have to go [check]." Swann said, later elaborating that "there's obligations to put your best team out there."

Greg Swann says teams have an obligation to try their best. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

On Monday the AFL attempted to provide more clarity, sending a memo to all 18 league clubs to remind them to "perform to their merits". As per Fox Footy, the memo referred clubs to league rules about performance and trying.

"Please be reminded of the obligation in the AFL Rules on Clubs to "perform on one's merits", meaning that Clubs must perform honestly and to the best of their ability," the memo read.

"While legitimate management of player fatigue and injuries is permitted, the AFL will scrutinise Club team selection decisions in the lead-up to the AFL Finals in the context of this Rule."

This memo caused a mild uproar across clubs, coaches and fans, hijacking much of the conversation of the week.

"I think the main consideration for the teams who might be certainties to play a wildcard game is the fact that the six teams above seventh all have a week off," Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge told Fox Footy on Monday.

Luke Beveridge will not be swayed on his selection choices. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

One of his potential finals rivals, Melbourne coach Steven King, also weighed in strongly.

"I'm the coach of the Melbourne footy club. I'll make any decision that's best for our football club and best for the management of our players," King said.

The AFL warns clubs they risk being sanctioned should they rest players in round 24, but several coaches say they will not be paying attention to the memo.

While much of the focus of the memo this season appears to be on sides that are preparing for finals, the rule also applies to those set to take a long September sojourn.

The spectre of tanking and strategic resting in football was once rife, with unproven allegations that several clubs performed to less than their merits in order to earn better (and more) draft picks.

The removal of clear guidelines around priority picks quietened this chat, but it has never fully gone away. Likewise, the mass-resting of players by North Melbourne and Fremantle about a decade ago spurred the AFL to institute a pre-finals bye.

Changes to the AFL's finals structure and to the draft compensation awarded to the league's weakest teams, may have renewed motivation to stretch the AFL's rules — and the patience of its fans — to its limits.

Teams are being encouraged to perform to their merits, whatever that entails. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

To find out what the AFL means by "performing on one's merits" you first need to crack out one of the core documents that governs the league — the AFL Rules. The Rules — not to be confused with the Laws of the Game — sets out how the AFL administers the league across 191 breezy pages.

It's in the middle of the definitions section that the league defines what they actually mean:

Perform on one's Merits: at all times to perform honestly and to the best of one's ability in the pursuit only of legitimate competitive objectives. For the avoidance of doubt "legitimate competitive objective" includes the development of the team or players or management of player fatigue or injuries but does not include improving a Club's draft position, improving a Club's position with respect to a potential Player exchange or manipulating a Club's position on the ladder for the purpose of improving its draw within the Finals Series.

The definition is both broad and narrow, vague and specific. The league puts that definition into action in two different sections of the Rules — Rule 29 and Rule 32.

Most of the time it's rule 29 that is considered when looking at sides performing to their merits. That rule relates to the operations of the draft, and more specifically "conduct prejudicial to the Draft". In real, non-lawyer speak that means tanking and tanking adjacent decisions. Rule 29 has a set series of penalties and procedures, and has been called into action previously — more on that later.

But it's rule 32 that's more interesting. That rule — called "Gambling" — looks at acts that are prohibited in the bookmaking space. That includes ensuring that:

In relation to any Match, aspect of a Match, or pre-Match planning and tactics, a Player, Coach or member of the Match Committee must at all times Perform on their Merits.

This section is even broader to its operations, with penalties handed out by the AFL Commission or General Counsel as they see fit. Rule 32 is more concerned with bulk resting before finals rather than sheer tanking, but more broadly ensures that the game is fair to uphold the obligations the league has to gambling markets.

So a team has to perform to their merits, unless their players are hurt or tired. Finding a better match in finals isn't a valid reason for failing to meet those standards, nor is securing a better draft pick.

But more broadly, does tanking, and resting up, stack up as strategy?

The Houston Rockets potentially tanked in 1983/1984 to take Hakeem Olajuwon (right) with the number one draft pick. Chicago claimed Michael Jordan (left) with the third pick. (Getty Images)

Tanking is not a new concept to the league, nor to sports that utilise drafts. But it's also not always successful — either in the short term or the long term.

It is generally believed that the first instance of tanking in sport occurred in the 1983/1984 NBA season.

In that season the Houston Rockets had eyes on Hakeem Olajuwon, a young Nigerian centre from the nearby University of Houston.

The team started the season strongly before fading late, making some questionable decisions along the way.

That stretch of futility afforded the Rockets with a coin flip to secure the top pick — one which landed their way.

The Rockets got their man, with The Dream eventually leading Houston to two titles and a brief stint as the best basketball player in the world on his way to the Basketball Hall of Fame.

However, Olajuwon didn't end up as the best player in that draft.

Two picks later the Chicago Bulls tabbed a 6'6" guard named Michael Jordan, who had a handy career of his own.

Sides in all four of the major US sports have tanked their way to title winning stars and cores — but not all sides have succeeded. While rumours of tanking abounded for years, it took some time for the phenomenon to firmly hit these shores.

In the AFL, tanking isn't just about securing the number one pick.

The number one pick is rarely the best player in the draft, or even often better than the second overall pick. The floor is higher than almost every other selection, but it's hard to pick who will be the single best player from looking at kids aged 17 or younger.

The most commonly cited examples of AFL tanking coincide with the era of defined priority draft picks.

Between the years of 1992 and 2012 teams received a draft pick at the start of the first round if they won very few games — five or less before 2005, and four or less in two consecutive seasons before between 2006 and 2012.

Not all the teams who received priority picks did so via tanking, but there are a small subset who have faced closer scrutiny.

In 2012 former Melbourne player Brock McLean gave an interview alleging that Melbourne made decisions around the selection and positioning of players that lessened the chances of victory for the club in 2009.

"Well, they don't call it tanking — we were calling it experimenting or whatever it was — and it just went against everything I was taught as a kid, taught as a footballer, as a person," McLean told Fox Footy's On The Couch.

Brock McLean says Melbourne did not tank, but "experimented". (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

After the interview the AFL opened a seven-month investigation. While the league cleared the club of tanking, it found the Demons had acted in a manner "prejudicial to the interests of the AFL".

The club was fined $500,000, with former staffers Chris Connolly and Dean Bailey serving suspensions from AFL duties.

The Demons were far from the only club to raise eyebrows for how closely to their merits they were performing.

Former Brownlow medallist and Carlton assistant coach Tony Liberatore alleged that Carlton had also considered future draft picks when making experimental late season selections in 2007.

In 2010 West Coast coach John Worsfold was clear that experimenting with selecting young players in unfamiliar positions was not tanking.

Neither side was sanctioned by the league. Both received priority picks. Rumours have existed about how closely to their merits other sides have performed in recent years, but no known formal action has been taken.

But one part of the equation is far more clear.

The allure of a priority pick was worthy of extreme action. Despite Melbourne tabbing Tom Scully and Jack Trengove ahead of Dustin Martin in that fateful 2009 draft, other clubs have used those picks to kickstart a swift rise up the ladder.

The gains from a coveted priority pick have been enormous at times — think Hawthorn securing a bonus Lance Franklin at pick five in addition to taking Jarryd Roughead at two, or Collingwood adding Scott Pendlebury to go with Dale Thomas.

Of the 17 occasions in which a club has earned very high priority picks, the majority made finals in the next few years.

Three teams won flags within five years, with the Judd/Sampi, Roughhead/Franklin and Pendlebury/Thomas pick combinations featuring prominently in multiple grand finals and premiership success.

Some second round priority picks, such as Alex Rance and Jack Darling, also proved critical to premiership pushes.

After 2012 the league changed the criteria for awarding priority picks, making them discretionary.

Since then, the Suns, Lions and Roos have been awarded assistance packages, with two of those three rising to finals shortly after gaining assistance.

While the priority pick rules haven't changed for 2026, another rule has been introduced that may further induce the need to experiment late in the year.

Dale Thomas and Scott Pendlebury made a dynamic pairing for Collingwood. (Getty Images: Robert Prezioso)

At the start of the year the AFL introduced a series of draft reforms designed to make the draft — and distribution of young talent across the league — fairer.

Matching bids for father-son and academy talents has got harder for clubs.

At the same time, clubs holding high draft picks at the top end of the draft now receive compensation (at the start of the second round) for club-tied players bid on (and matched) early.

Clubs holding their natural draft picks whose picks are pushed down the order now receive a compensation selection at the start of the second round of the draft, if they go on to pick a player with their original selection.

While this is not as generous as the previous priority pick regime, an extra pick could incentivise finishing 14th over 13th if finals are off the table.

A fresh, early second round pick is more likely to be worthy of a tank than the mere difference between pick one and two.

While many have raised North Melbourne's late season win in 2023 that cost the club the chance to select Harley Reid, the young Eagle has yet to fully cement himself as the most valuable player of that draft class.

Indeed, heading into that draft, some clubs tabbed Jed Walter as the most talented player in the class, albeit one that was firmly off limits due to his ties to the Suns.

The race for the fifth pick appears to be heading down to the wire, with the Suns, Roos and Giants all in the mix for the last choice.

If the Suns finish fifth, no compensation pick will be generated due to the pick already being traded to Melbourne.

Jed Walter was always tied to the Suns through the 2023 draft class. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

There's now also a stronger incentive for clubs with tied talent to ensure they have enough points to match any bid — or to sneak a pick in before a bid comes in.

For example, Carlton's late season surge has made the battle to get likely top three draft pick Cody Walker to the club harder.

If the Blues finish inside the top 10 they will not receive a discount on matching a potential bid, alongside having a worse hand to match with.

Time will tell if these sides — and others — experiment more in the last three weeks of the season.

Then there's what many people noted as the original intent of the AFL's memo — the locked-in finals teams.

While the finals have expanded and the bye week before finals removed, the week off is still functionally there for the top six sides, with the top four eyeing two weeks off in a three week period.

As a result it's the sides placed 7 through 10 with reasons to make sure their players are rested for a deep run in finals. Wildcard teams face the prospect of winning five straight games to win a long shot premiership, and can only be expected to eke out every little advantage facing such a gauntlet.

A week off isn't automatically an advantage for football teams — statistics show no advantage for teams coming off a bye in the middle of the year.

It's likely that team circumstances vary too much for planned byes to have consistent influence.

One club may benefit from a rest, extra player rehab, and renewed energy to help them reset and succeed, while another may find the danger of upsetting their rhythm and getting a bit rusty.

However, later in the year, when teams are banged up and facing the step up to finals level intensity, a week without football is more likely to appear as a boon for many players.

Players are dropping down with injuries during this longest AFL season ever. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

Even considering all of these factors, many will be asking why the AFL released this memo now.

The risks outlined above aren't down to changes made in the last week or month, or unforeseen circumstances.

The 2026 season is one of the longest on record. By the end of the year, most players will be battling niggles, injuries or fatigue.

As per the AFL Rules, these are valid reasons for players to be rested. In addition, the rules encouraging players, staffers and teams to "perform to one's merits" have rarely been tested, if ever.

For many clubs and fans, the concept of acceptable losses and tanking runs contrary to the entire concept of sport.

This is similar to the teachings of Canadian philosopher Shorsey, who exalted that the most important thing is not that players don't love to win, but that they hate to lose.

The tears shed by West Coast's Willem Duursma speaks to this anguish at loss, and what drives the best to the next level.

Instead, the memo appears to be an AFL attempt to control a developing media cycle.

Rather than quietening discontent, it seemed to accelerate the uncertainty — including amongst the coaching cohort.

A clearer initial answer from the league may have headed the conversation off at the pass.

In the end, the only added dimension may be fans now trying to guess the ultimate intentions of teams with ground to gain at the margins — regardless of whether they are trying to do so or not.
